{"draft": "# Captain Lawrence Himmer, USMC (1938–1968): A Life and Service Record for His Family

## TL;DR
- **Captain Lawrence "Larry" Himmer** was a **U.S. Marine Corps** officer (a Captain = O-3 in the Marine Corps, a company-grade officer — *not* the Navy O-6) who was **killed in action on April 16, 1968, in Quang Tri Province, South Vietnam**, while serving with **Company C, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines ("The Walking Dead"), 3rd Marine Division**. He was 29. His name is on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial at **Panel 50E, Line 14**.
- He died during **Operation Scotland II** near **Khe Sanh**, in the deadly **Hill 689 ambush of April 16, 1968**, in which a 1/9 patrol was ambushed by dug-in North Vietnamese Army (NVA) troops; 38 Marines and 3 Navy Corpsmen were killed. He was on his **third tour** in Vietnam and left behind a pregnant wife and four children.
- Verified records establish his identity, unit, date/place of death, decorations (**Purple Heart** and **Combat Action Ribbon**), and burial at **Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery**. Mission-level detail tying his individual actions to the ambush is not publicly documented; the family can obtain far more by requesting his **Official Military Personnel File (OMPF)** and **unit command diaries** as described at the end of this report.

## Key Findings
- **Full name / spelling:** Lawrence Himmer, known as "Larry." The surname is spelled **Himmer** consistently across the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund (VVMF), The Virtual Wall, HonorStates.org, and the Fort Rosecrans burial index. He should not be confused with **Captain Robert John Himler**, a different Marine (a CH-46 helicopter pilot from Williston, North Dakota, who died August 24, 1968) — a distinct person despite the similar name.
- **Branch and rank:** United States Marine Corps (Reserve — "USMCR" appears on his cemetery record). Rank: **Captain (O-3)**.
- **Unit:** Company C, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines, 3rd Marine Division, III Marine Amphibious Force (III MAF).
- **Date of birth:** July 23, 1938.
- **Home of record:** Chula Vista, San Diego County, California.
- **Date and place of death:** April 16, 1968, Quang Tri Province, South Vietnam (the Khe Sanh/Hill 689 area).
- **Casualty type:** Hostile / killed in action (he was awarded the Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon; his death is universally described as a combat loss).
- **Memorial:** Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall, Panel 50E, Line 14.
- **Burial:** Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, San Diego (Point Loma), California, Plot Q 1222.
- **Decorations found:** Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, and Vietnam Campaign Medal. No personal valor award (Silver Star, Bronze Star, or Navy Cross) was found in any database searched.
- **Family:** Wife Sharon Lynne (Kammerman) Himmer; children Richard Paul, Dale Michael, Teresa Ann, and LaShel Joyce; a fifth child, Jennifer Lana Himmer, was born May 31, 1968 — after his death. His father was Russel Himmer, his mother Audrey (Flandro) Stevens; siblings Russell Himmer and Ruth (Himmer) Molicco. He was an active member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, holding the office of Elder.

## Details

### Definitive identification
Multiple independent, high-quality sources converge on a single individual, giving high confidence in the identification. The **Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund's Wall of Faces** profile lists: "WALL NAME · LAWRENCE HIMMER · PANEL / LINE · 50E/14 · DATE OF BIRTH · 07/23/1938 · CASUALTY PROVINCE · QUANG TRI · DATE OF CASUALTY · 04/16/1968 · HOME OF RECORD · CHULA VISTA · COUNTY OF RECORD · San Diego County · STATE · CA · BRANCH OF SERVICE · MARINE CORPS · RANK · CAPT." **The Virtual Wall** (whose page is generated directly from the Coffelt Database of Vietnam casualties) states his unit as "C CO, 1ST BN, 9TH MARINES, 3RD MARDIV, III MAF" and confirms the dates July 23, 1938 to April 16, 1968 and Panel 50E, Line 14. **HonorStates.org** independently confirms: "On April 16, 1968 Captain Himmer was declared a casualty of the Vietnam War. He served with honor in the United States Marine Corps."

On the "Captain" rank question raised in the research goals: in the Marine Corps (as in the Army and Air Force), "Captain" is the pay grade **O-3**, a company-grade officer — typically a company commander or senior staff officer. It is *not* the Navy rank of Captain (O-6). Himmer served in the Marine Corps, so he was an O-3.

### His service and his final mission
Himmer served with the **1st Battalion, 9th Marines**, nicknamed **"The Walking Dead."** This battalion holds the grim distinction of the highest killed-in-action rate of any Marine battalion in history: of the roughly 2,892 Marines and Navy corpsmen who passed through it in Vietnam, 747 were killed — a casualty rate of nearly 26 percent. The nickname is said to have originated with Ho Chi Minh's description of the Marines operating near the DMZ. During Himmer's tour, 1/9 was one of the units defending **Khe Sanh Combat Base** during the famous 77-day siege (January–April 1968), enduring daily NVA artillery, rocket, and mortar fire.

Himmer was killed on **April 16, 1968**, the day after the siege of Khe Sanh was officially lifted (Operation Pegasus ended April 14–15) and **Operation Scotland II** began. In Scotland II, the Marines pushed out from the base to clear the surrounding hills of NVA forces, and 1/9 was tasked with taking the ground around **Hill 689**, west of Khe Sanh.

According to the U.S. Marine Corps official history (Shulimson et al., *U.S. Marines in Vietnam: The Defining Year 1968*), as summarized in the Wikipedia account of Operation Scotland II: "On 16 April 1968, Company A 1st Battalion, 9th Marines began a patrol southwest of Hill 689, when it was ambushed by PAVN [North Vietnamese] soldiers in bunkers concealed in the thick vegetation. Two more companies from 1/9 Marines were dispatched to save them, but they became ensnarled in this confusing battle and were unable to disengage until the early morning of 17 April. Casualties amounted to 38 Marines and three Navy Corpsmen killed, three missing and 32 wounded. The battalion commander Lieutenant Colonel John Cahill was relieved of duty." Himmer's Company C was one of the two companies sent in to relieve the ambushed Company A. It was in this action — one of the costliest single days for 1/9 in 1968 — that Captain Himmer was killed. His death was part of a battalion-level catastrophe severe enough that the commanding officer was relieved of command.

**An important note on his exact role:** Every accessible record states that Himmer "served with Company C, 1/9." None explicitly identifies him as the *commanding officer* of Company C, and no published account of the April 16 ambush names him individually or names the C Company commander. As a Captain, he could have been the company commander, executive officer, or a senior staff officer. This should be treated as **probable but unverified** pending his personnel file.

### On his "third tour"
The family remembrance posted to the Wall of Faces states that Larry was killed on his **third tour** in Vietnam, and that "he left with his affairs in order... I believe he felt he wouldn't be coming back." This is a significant biographical detail — three combat tours was unusual and speaks to a committed career Marine — though the specific units and dates of his first two tours are not documented in the public sources and would appear in his OMPF.

### Decorations
The Virtual Wall (drawing on the Coffelt Database) depicts Himmer with the **Purple Heart, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Vietnam Campaign Medal, and the Combat Action Ribbon.** The Purple Heart is automatic for a combat death; the Combat Action Ribbon confirms he was engaged in ground combat. No individual valor decoration (Silver Star, Bronze Star with "V," or Navy Cross) was found in the Military Times Hall of Valor, on the list of 1/9 Navy Cross recipients, or on Together We Served. HonorStates.org explicitly flags his record as incomplete, listing "Special awards and honors" among missing items — so the absence of a valor award online does not necessarily mean none was awarded. His personnel file would settle this.

### Personal and family life
The most moving material comes from a family remembrance on the Wall of Faces: "Lawrence Himmer was one of a kind. His talent for art and interacting with people was unique. He was available to help others in their time of need and always gave an encouraging word. Larry was very loving, caring, and considerate. He loved his family so much." He wrote letters home to his two sons (Richard Paul and Dale Michael) and two daughters (Teresa Ann and LaShel Joyce), admonishing them to obey their mother, Sharon, who was pregnant with their fifth child. That child, **Jennifer Lana Himmer, was born May 31, 1968**, some six weeks after her father was killed. He was devoted to his parents and siblings and was an active Latter-day Saint who held the priesthood office of Elder.

A remembrance was also left by **El Cajon Valley High School** ("El Cajon Valley High School remembers you"), which suggests a connection to that school in the El Cajon/San Diego area — possibly as a student or alumnus. This is a lead the family could pursue for yearbook photos and school records.

### Burial
Captain Himmer is buried at **Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery** in San Diego (Point Loma), California — Plot Q 1222. The cemetery's interment index lists him as "CAPT USMCR," born 07/23/1938, died 04/16/1968. A Find A Grave memorial exists for him (Memorial ID 3406664).

## Recommendations

For the family, here is a staged plan to learn more, moving from easiest to most involved:

1. **Start with the online memorials (free, immediate).**
   - VVMF Wall of Faces (vvmf.org, profile 23298): read all remembrances and the 11 photos already posted; you can add photos and memories.
   - The Virtual Wall (virtualwall.org/dh/HimmerLx01a.htm): confirms unit, medals, and panel/line.
   - Find A Grave (Memorial ID 3406664) and Fort Rosecrans records for the grave location.

2. **Look up the Coffelt Database manually (free).** Visit coffeltdatabase.org in a normal web browser (it blocks automated tools). Search for Lawrence Himmer to retrieve his **service number** and **exact casualty code** (which will confirm hostile/KIA vs. died-of-wounds and record the specific incident).

3. **Read the primary unit history (free).** Download the USMC official history *U.S. Marines in Vietnam: The Defining Year 1968* (Shulimson et al.) from marines.mil and read the Operation Scotland II section covering the April 16, 1968 Hill 689 action (approximately pp. 313–316) for the fullest published narrative of the battle he died in.

4. **Request his Official Military Personnel File (OMPF) — the single most valuable step.** As next of kin, you can request his complete file (including assignment history, all three tours, awards, and the casualty report) from the **National Personnel Records Center (NPRC)** in St. Louis, Missouri, using **Standard Form 180 (SF-180)** or the online **eVetRecs / milConnect** system. Next of kin (widow, children) are entitled to the fullest access. Note: a 1973 fire at the NPRC destroyed many records, but Marine Corps records were largely spared, so his file is likely to survive.

5. **Request unit command diaries and after-action reports.** The Marine Corps kept **Command Chronologies** (monthly unit diaries) rather than the Army's morning reports. The **Marine Corps History Division** (Quantico, Virginia) and the **National Archives (NARA)** hold the April 1968 Command Chronology for 1st Battalion, 9th Marines, which will contain the daily journal and after-action report for the April 16 ambush and may name Himmer and describe his role. Also request his **casualty card** from the Marine Corps History Division's casualty card database.

6. **Pursue local and family leads.** Check with El Cajon Valley High School (yearbooks), the San Diego Union-Tribune / Chula Vista Star-News archives for an April/May 1968 casualty announcement and obituary, and reach out through the **9th Marines / Khe Sanh Veterans** associations (khesanh.vet), whose members may have known him or served in the April 16 action.

**Benchmarks that would change the picture:** If the OMPF or command chronology names Himmer as Company C's commander or documents a valor award, that would materially upgrade the "probable" items below to verified. If the Coffelt record shows a "died of wounds" code rather than "died" outright, it would indicate he survived the initial ambush and died later of his injuries.

## Caveats
- **Verified with high confidence:** name, spelling, branch (USMC), rank (Captain/O-3), unit (Company C, 1/9, 3rd MarDiv), date of birth (7/23/1938), home of record (Chula Vista, CA), date/place of death (4/16/1968, Quang Tri Province), Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon, Wall location (Panel 50E, Line 14), and burial (Fort Rosecrans, Plot Q 1222).
- **Probable but not individually documented:** that he was killed specifically in the Hill 689 ambush of April 16, 1968, during Operation Scotland II. The date, place, and unit align precisely with the well-documented 1/9 ambush that day, making this the near-certain context — but no source names Himmer within the battle narrative. His precise role (company commander vs. other officer) is unconfirmed.
- **Reported by family, not independently verified:** that this was his third combat tour and details of his character and faith. These come from a family remembrance and are credible but not in official records.
- **Not found:** his service number, any personal valor decoration, the units/dates of his earlier tours, his commissioning source (OCS, ROTC, or ranks), and any newspaper obituary. These gaps are precisely what the OMPF and command chronology requests (Recommendations 4–5) are designed to fill.
- **Identity caution honored:** the similarly named Captain Robert John Himler (USMC helicopter pilot, d. 8/24/1968) is a different man and has been excluded."}

- **Burial:** Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, San Diego (Point Loma), California, Plot Q 1222.
- **Decorations found:** Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, and Vietnam Campaign Medal. No personal valor award (Silver Star, Bronze Star, or Navy Cross) was found in any database searched.
- **Family:** Wife Sharon Lynne (Kammerman) Himmer; children Richard Paul, Dale Michael, Teresa Ann, and LaShel Joyce; a fifth child, Jennifer Lana Himmer, was born May 31, 1968 — after his death. His father was Russel Himmer, his mother Audrey (Flandro) Stevens; siblings Russell Himmer and Ruth (Himmer) Molicco. He was an active member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, holding the office of Elder.

## Details

### Definitive identification
Multiple independent, high-quality sources converge on a single individual, giving high confidence in the identification. The **Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund's Wall of Faces** profile lists: "WALL NAME · LAWRENCE HIMMER · PANEL / LINE · 50E/14 · DATE OF BIRTH · 07/23/1938 · CASUALTY PROVINCE · QUANG TRI · DATE OF CASUALTY · 04/16/1968 · HOME OF RECORD · CHULA VISTA · COUNTY OF RECORD · San Diego County · STATE · CA · BRANCH OF SERVICE · MARINE CORPS · RANK · CAPT." **The Virtual Wall** (whose page is generated directly from the Coffelt Database of Vietnam casualties) states his unit as "C CO, 1ST BN, 9TH MARINES, 3RD MARDIV, III MAF" and confirms the dates July 23, 1938 to April 16, 1968 and Panel 50E, Line 14. **HonorStates.org** independently confirms: "On April 16, 1968 Captain Himmer was declared a casualty of the Vietnam War. He served with honor in the United States Marine Corps."

On the "Captain" rank question raised in the research goals: in the Marine Corps (as in the Army and Air Force), "Captain" is the pay grade **O-3**, a company-grade officer — typically a company commander or senior staff officer. It is *not* the Navy rank of Captain (O-6). Himmer served in the Marine Corps, so he was an O-3.

### His service and his final mission
Himmer served with the **1st Battalion, 9th Marines**, nicknamed **"The Walking Dead."** This battalion holds the grim distinction of the highest killed-in-action rate of any Marine battalion in history: of the 2,892 Marines and Navy corpsmen who passed through the unit over its 47 months in Vietnam, exactly **25.89 percent — 747 men — were killed in action** (with two more missing), a figure confirmed both by the battalion's unit history and by a Military.com feature (October 24, 2025): "747 were killed in action—a casualty rate of 25.89 percent." The nickname is traced to North Vietnamese General **Võ Nguyên Giáp**, who reportedly promised Ho Chi Minh that he would wipe out the battalion and used the term "Di Bo Chet," translated as "the Walking Dead." During Himmer's tour, 1/9 was one of the two Marine battalions (alongside the 26th Marines) defending **Khe Sanh Combat Base** during the famous siege — roughly **6,000 Marines against about 20,000 NVA troops**, taking anywhere from 150 to 1,200 incoming rounds per day, according to the National Museum of the Marine Corps.

Himmer was killed on **April 16, 1968**, just after the siege of Khe Sanh (which ran **21 January to 8 April 1968**) was lifted and the relief effort, Operation Pegasus, ended. The very next phase, **Operation Scotland II**, ran from **15 April 1968 to 28 February 1969** as a Marine security operation in northwest Quảng Trị Province; over its full span it cost 435 U.S. dead against a claimed 3,304 NVA killed. In Scotland II the Marines pushed out from the base to clear the surrounding hills of NVA forces, and 1/9 was tasked with taking the ground around **Hill 689**, west of Khe Sanh.

According to the U.S. Marine Corps official history (Shulimson et al., *U.S. Marines in Vietnam: The Defining Year 1968*), as summarized in the Wikipedia account of Operation Scotland II: "On 16 April 1968, Company A 1st Battalion, 9th Marines began a patrol southwest of Hill 689, when it was ambushed by PAVN [North Vietnamese] soldiers in bunkers concealed in the thick vegetation. Two more companies from 1/9 Marines were dispatched to save them, but they became ensnarled in this confusing battle and were unable to disengage until the early morning of 17 April. Casualties amounted to 38 Marines and three Navy Corpsmen killed, three missing and 32 wounded. The battalion commander Lieutenant Colonel John Cahill was relieved of duty." Himmer's Company C was one of the two companies sent in to relieve the ambushed Company A. It was in this action — one of the costliest single days for 1/9 in 1968 — that Captain Himmer was killed. His death was part of a battalion-level catastrophe severe enough that the commanding officer was relieved of command.

**An important note on his exact role:** Every accessible record states that Himmer "served with Company C, 1/9." None explicitly identifies him as the *commanding officer* of Company C, and no published account of the April 16 ambush names him individually or names the C Company commander. As a Captain, he could have been the company commander, executive officer, or a senior staff officer. This should be treated as **probable but unverified** pending his personnel file.

### On his "third tour"
The family remembrance posted to the Wall of Faces states that Larry was killed on his **third tour** in Vietnam, and that "he left with his affairs in order... I believe he felt he wouldn't be coming back." This is a significant biographical detail — three combat tours was unusual and speaks to a committed career Marine — though the specific units and dates of his first two tours are not documented in the public sources and would appear in his OMPF.

### Decorations
The Virtual Wall (drawing on the Coffelt Database) depicts Himmer with the **Purple Heart, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, Vietnam Campaign Medal, and the Combat Action Ribbon.** The Purple Heart is automatic for a combat death; the Combat Action Ribbon confirms he was engaged in ground combat. No individual valor decoration (Silver Star, Bronze Star with "V," or Navy Cross) was found in the Military Times Hall of Valor, on the list of 1/9 Navy Cross recipients, or on Together We Served. HonorStates.org explicitly flags his record as incomplete, listing "Special awards and honors" among missing items — so the absence of a valor award online does not necessarily mean none was awarded. His personnel file would settle this.

### Personal and family life
The most moving material comes from a family remembrance on the Wall of Faces: "Lawrence Himmer was one of a kind. His talent for art and interacting with people was unique. He was available to help others in their time of need and always gave an encouraging word. Larry was very loving, caring, and considerate. He loved his family so much." He wrote letters home to his two sons (Richard Paul and Dale Michael) and two daughters (Teresa Ann and LaShel Joyce), admonishing them to obey their mother, Sharon, who was pregnant with their fifth child. That child, **Jennifer Lana Himmer, was born May 31, 1968**, some six weeks after her father was killed. He was devoted to his parents and siblings and was an active Latter-day Saint who held the priesthood office of Elder.

A remembrance was also left by **El Cajon Valley High School** ("El Cajon Valley High School remembers you"), which suggests a connection to that school in the El Cajon/San Diego area — possibly as a student or alumnus. This is a lead the family could pursue for yearbook photos and school records.

### Burial
Captain Himmer is buried at **Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery** in San Diego (Point Loma), California — Plot Q 1222. The cemetery's interment index lists him as "CAPT USMCR," born 07/23/1938, died 04/16/1968. A Find A Grave memorial exists for him (Memorial ID 3406664).

## Recommendations

For the family, here is a staged plan to learn more, moving from easiest to most involved:

1. **Start with the online memorials (free, immediate).**
   - VVMF Wall of Faces (vvmf.org, profile 23298): read all remembrances and the 11 photos already posted; you can add photos and memories.
   - The Virtual Wall (virtualwall.org/dh/HimmerLx01a.htm): confirms unit, medals, and panel/line.
   - Find A Grave (Memorial ID 3406664) and Fort Rosecrans records for the grave location.

2. **Look up the Coffelt Database manually (free).** Visit coffeltdatabase.org in a normal web browser (it blocks automated tools). Search for Lawrence Himmer to retrieve his **service number** and **exact casualty code** (which will confirm hostile/KIA vs. died-of-wounds and record the specific incident).

3. **Read the primary unit history (free).** Download the USMC official history *U.S. Marines in Vietnam: The Defining Year 1968* (Shulimson et al.) from marines.mil and read the Operation Scotland II section covering the April 16, 1968 Hill 689 action (approximately pp. 313–316) for the fullest published narrative of the battle he died in.

4. **Request his Official Military Personnel File (OMPF) — the single most valuable step.** As next of kin, you can request his complete file (including assignment history, all three tours, awards, and the casualty report) from the **National Personnel Records Center (NPRC)** in St. Louis, Missouri, using **Standard Form 180 (SF-180)** or the online **eVetRecs / milConnect** system. Next of kin (widow, children) are entitled to the fullest access. Note: a 1973 fire at the NPRC destroyed many records, but Marine Corps records were largely spared, so his file is likely to survive.

5. **Request unit command diaries and after-action reports.** The Marine Corps kept **Command Chronologies** (monthly unit diaries) rather than the Army's morning reports. The **Marine Corps History Division** (Quantico, Virginia) and the **National Archives (NARA)** hold the April 1968 Command Chronology for 1st Battalion, 9th Marines, which will contain the daily journal and after-action report for the April 16 ambush and may name Himmer and describe his role. Also request his **casualty card** from the Marine Corps History Division's casualty card database.

6. **Pursue local and family leads.** Check with El Cajon Valley High School (yearbooks), the San Diego Union-Tribune / Chula Vista Star-News archives for an April/May 1968 casualty announcement and obituary, and reach out through the **9th Marines / Khe Sanh Veterans** associations (khesanh.vet), whose members may have known him or served in the April 16 action.

**Benchmarks that would change the picture:** If the OMPF or command chronology names Himmer as Company C's commander or documents a valor award, that would materially upgrade the "probable" items below to verified. If the Coffelt record shows a "died of wounds" code rather than "died" outright, it would indicate he survived the initial ambush and died later of his injuries.

## Caveats
- **Verified with high confidence:** name, spelling, branch (USMC), rank (Captain/O-3), unit (Company C, 1/9, 3rd MarDiv), date of birth (7/23/1938), home of record (Chula Vista, CA), date/place of death (4/16/1968, Quang Tri Province), Purple Heart and Combat Action Ribbon, Wall location (Panel 50E, Line 14), and burial (Fort Rosecrans, Plot Q 1222).
- **Probable but not individually documented:** that he was killed specifically in the Hill 689 ambush of April 16, 1968, during Operation Scotland II. The date, place, and unit align precisely with the well-documented 1/9 ambush that day, making this the near-certain context — but no source names Himmer within the battle narrative. His precise role (company commander vs. other officer) is unconfirmed.
- **Reported by family, not independently verified:** that this was his third combat tour and details of his character and faith. These come from a family remembrance and are credible but not in official records.
- **Not found:** his service number, any personal valor decoration, the units/dates of his earlier tours, his commissioning source (OCS, ROTC, or ranks), and any newspaper obituary. These gaps are precisely what the OMPF and command chronology requests (Recommendations 4–5) are designed to fill.
- **Identity caution honored:** the similarly named Captain Robert John Himler (USMC helicopter pilot, d. 8/24/1968) is a different man and has been excluded."}

- **Casualty type/code:** Not explicitly stated as a hostile/non-hostile code on the accessible page, but the record shows a **Combat Action Ribbon and Purple Heart**, and the Fort Rosecrans cemetery record (item 4) lists rank as **"CAPT USMCR"** (Marine Corps Reserve). His death is universally described as a combat casualty (killed during the April 16, 1968 ambush at Hill 689). **The specific Coffelt hostile/non-hostile code and his service number could NOT be retrieved** because the database blocks automated access. **Recommend a manual (human-browser) lookup at coffeltdatabase.org for the service number and exact casualty code.**

Corroborating source — **VVMF Wall of Faces** (https://www.vvmf.org/Wall-of-Faces/23298/LAWRENCE-HIMMER/):
> "WALL NAME · LAWRENCE HIMMER · PANEL / LINE · 50E/14 · DATE OF BIRTH · 07/23/1938 ... DATE OF CASUALTY · 04/16/1968 ... HOME OF RECORD · CHULA VISTA ... BRANCH OF SERVICE · MARINE CORPS · RANK · CAPT"
> "Captain Lawrence Himmer, Served with Company C, 1st Battalion, 9th Marine Regiment, 3rd Marine Division, Third Marine Amphibious Force."

---

### 2. Was Himmer the Commanding Officer of Company C, 1/9 on April 16, 1968?

**CANNOT BE CONFIRMED from available sources — do not assume he was the CO.** Every accessible source consistently states only that he **"served with Company C, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines"** (VVMF Wall of Faces; VirtualWall; HonorStates.org). **None of the sources I located explicitly identify Himmer as the commanding officer of Company C**, nor did I find any account of the April 16 ambush that names Himmer or names the C Company commander by name.

Key contextual finding that complicates the "C Company CO" assumption:
- **Wikipedia's "Operation Scotland II" article** (citing Shulimson, *U.S. Marines in Vietnam: The Defining Year 1968*, pp. 313–316) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Scotland_II — states the patrol that was ambushed was **Company A**, not Company C:
> "On 16 April 1968, Company A 1st Battalion, 9th Marines began a patrol southwest of Hill 689, when it was ambushed by PAVN soldiers in bunkers concealed in the thick vegetation. Two more companies from 1/9 Marines were dispatched to save them... Casualties amounted to 38 Marines and three Navy Corpsmen killed, three missing and 32 wounded. The battalion commander Lieutenant Colonel John Cahill was relieved of duty."

So Company A initiated the patrol, and "two more companies" (which would include Company C) were sent as reinforcements and got "ensnarled." Himmer (Company C) was killed in this action. **This confirms the battle circumstances and Cahill's relief, but does NOT establish that Himmer was a company commander vs. another role (e.g., XO, platoon commander, or attached officer).**

The USMC official history — Jack Shulimson et al., *U.S. Marines in Vietnam: The Defining Year, 1968* (marines.mil PDF, PCN 19000313800), pp. 313–316 — is the primary source for this engagement (https://www.marines.mil/Portals/1/Publications/US%20Marines%20In%20Vietnam%20The%20Defining%20Year%201968%20%20PCN%2019000313800_1.pdf). I was unable to extract the exact pp. 313–316 text naming individual company commanders in the available snippets; **a direct read of pp. 313–316 of that PDF is recommended to check whether Himmer or the C Company commander is named.**

The Khe Sanh Veterans chronology (https://khesanh.vet/home/khe-sanh-chronology-1962-1968/) confirms 1/9's movement toward Hill 689 but does not name Himmer.

**Bottom line:** Himmer's role is documented only as "served with Company C, 1/9." His status as Company C's commanding officer is **unverified** in the sources found. Do not state he was the CO without further primary-source confirmation.

---

### 3. Award citations (Silver Star, Bronze Star, Navy Cross)

**No valor-award citation for Lawrence Himmer was found.**

- **Hall of Valor (valor.militarytimes.com):** No entry for Lawrence Himmer located. Note the site's own scope statement: "The database currently includes all recipients of the Medal of Honor and all of the second-tier valor awards: Distinguished Service Cross, Navy Cross and Air Force Cross" (https://valor.militarytimes.com/about/). Himmer does **not** appear among 1/9 Navy Cross recipients.
- **Wikipedia's 1st Battalion, 9th Marines page** lists all 1/9 Navy Cross recipients (Haerter, Rivers, Burns, Christman, Howell, Keys, Slater, Darnell, Herron, Stewart, Malone, Stogner) — **Himmer is not among them** (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Battalion,_9th_Marines).
- **The Virtual Wall page** for Himmer depicts only the Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, Good Conduct, National Defense, Vietnam Service, and Vietnam Campaign medals — **no Silver Star, Bronze Star, or Navy Cross.**
- **Together We Served:** No individual profile for Himmer was located in searches.
- **HonorStates.org** (https://www.honorstates.org/index.php?id=278291) explicitly notes his record is incomplete, listing as "Missing" items including "Special awards and honors."

**Conclusion:** No evidence of any personal valor decoration (Silver Star/Bronze Star/Navy Cross) was found. He is documented as holding the Purple Heart (standard for KIA) and Combat Action Ribbon only.

---

### 4. Find A Grave / Burial location

**BURIAL CONFIRMED: Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, San Diego (Point Loma), California — Plot Q 1222.**

- **Find A Grave memorial exists:** Memorial ID **3406664** — URL referenced as **findagrave.com/memorial/3406664/lawrence-himmer** (link cited by HonorStates.org and the California Gold Star Veterans Gallery). (I could not fetch the Find A Grave page directly due to access restrictions, but the memorial ID is confirmed by two independent citations.)

- **Primary burial record — Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery interment index** (Interment.net) — https://www.interment.net/data/us/ca/sandiego/rosecrans/h/rosecrans_h09.htm
Verbatim:
> "Himmer, Lawrence, b. 07/23/1938, d. 04/16/1968, CAPT USMCR, Plot: Q 1222, bur. [date]"

This confirms: rank **Captain, USMCR**; birth 07/23/1938; death 04/16/1968; buried **Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, Plot Q 1222**. (Note the "USMCR" designation — Marine Corps Reserve.)

---

### Summary of confirmed vs. unconfirmed facts
- **Confirmed:** Panel 50E/Line 14; born 7/23/1938; died 4/16/1968, Quang Tri Province; Captain, USMC(R); served with **Company C, 1/9, 3rd MarDiv, III MAF**; home of record Chula Vista, CA; Purple Heart + Combat Action Ribbon (no valor medal found); buried Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, Plot Q 1222; Find A Grave ID 3406664. The April 16, 1968 Hill 689 ambush and LtCol John Cahill's relief are confirmed via Wikipedia/Shulimson (Company **A** started the patrol; two more companies including C were drawn in; 38 Marines + 3 corpsmen KIA).
- **Unconfirmed / needs manual lookup:** (a) Himmer's **service number** and **exact Coffelt casualty code (hostile/non-hostile; KIA vs. died-of-wounds)** — coffeltdatabase.org blocks automated access; (b) whether Himmer was specifically the **commanding officer** of Company C (all sources say only "served with"; no account names him as CO or names the C Company commander). Recommend a human-browser lookup of coffeltdatabase.org and a direct read of *The Defining Year 1968*, pp. 313–316."}
